title: Small things first
hook: practice on small grievances before big ones

segments.voice: Yesterday, Witvliet's forgiveness and health: forgiving and lower stress show up together, though which causes which is still unclear. Your line was lighter. What did your shoulders do? Today the block turns from the research to practices. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

At the end of a rack of weights in a gym sits the lightest one, small enough to lift with two fingers. It's there on purpose. Muscles learn the movement on it before they're asked to carry anything heavy. Forgiveness tends to get talked about at the heavy end of the rack: betrayal, cruelty, the things that change a life. Those are real, and they matter. But the movement itself, noticing a hurt and letting it go, can be learned on something much lighter. This one starts at the other end of the rack. Today: small things first.
screen: `THE LIGHTEST WEIGHT IN THE RACK.` → `FORGIVENESS AT THE HEAVY END.` → `START AT THE OTHER END.`

segments.voice: First, an old Chinese voice. The Tao Te Ching, in its sixty-third chapter, says that the difficult things of the world are done while they are still easy, and the great things of the world while they are still small. In Chinese, the word for small there is xi: small, fine, slender. The great begins in the small. Second, a line from Luke's Gospel that says something close: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." The least comes first, and it isn't wasted practice. It's where the habit forms. Third, where the small things are. They're everywhere. The person who took the last coffee. The friend who was late again. The roommate who left the dishes. The comment in the group chat that stung a little. Grievances this size come along all day, which means the practice can too, several times before lunch. Each one is a chance to run the whole motion in miniature: notice it, name it plainly, and let it go. Fourth, what that builds. A motion done often becomes familiar. When something heavy does come, the movement of letting go isn't brand new; it has been rehearsed on small things, again and again. Starting small isn't a way of pretending the big wounds don't exist. And it doesn't put them on a schedule. Not yet is still allowed for those. It just means the first rep happens on the lightest weight in the rack.
screen: `THE GREAT BEGINS IN THE SMALL.` · `FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.` · `SMALL GRIEVANCES ARE EVERYWHERE.` · `THE SAME MOTION, REHEARSED.` · then, large: `START SMALL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Find one small grievance from the last day or two. The smaller the better: a door not held, a slow checkout, a dish left in the sink. Notice it. Name it plainly in one sentence. Then let it go, the way you'd set down the lightest weight in the rack, without ceremony. If another small one comes up, do the same again. Notice, name, release. The bell holds the time.
Xi. The Chinese word for small, fine, slender, from the Tao Te Ching's teaching that great things begin small. Today's word.
Your line: start small. Today, when the first small irritation arrives, run the whole motion once, right there: notice it, name it, let it go. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some forgiveness programs suggest practicing first on minor, everyday grievances, such as a rude remark or a late friend, before working on deeper hurts.

notes: Tao Te Ching 63 is paraphrased (not quoted from Legge, since the exact Legge wording wasn't certain). The Chinese line 天下大事，必作於細 and the gloss of 細 (xì) as small/fine/slender should be checked by a Chinese reader. Pronunciation 'SHEE' approximates xì.
'the sixty-third chapter' is the chapter number of the cited text.
howItsDone says 'some forgiveness programs'; no specific program is cited. A reviewer may want one (e.g., a Luskin or Worthington workbook) or to soften further.
